content.title: About
content.content: Light cream is a smooth dairy product with reduced fat content (typically 10‑15 %). It is made from skimmed milk, cream and stabilizers, providing a lower‑calorie option while retaining a creamy texture and mild taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light cream is often used in desserts where fewer calories are desired.
Unlike regular whipping cream, light cream may contain emulsifiers that keep the structure stable despite the low fat level.
In some countries light cream is classified as a "milk product" rather than a "cream".
It pairs well with berries, fruits, and whole‑grain baked goods.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Reduced fat makes the cream more suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Like other dairy products, light cream provides calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The cream contains vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Lower fat levels ease digestion, especially for people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: As a dairy product, light cream can cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Emulsifier additives
items.content: Some manufacturers use stabilizers that may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Flavored versions may contain added sugar, increasing the calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Light cream is suitable for spreading on bread, adding to coffee, mixing into fruit salads, desserts and light mousses. It can be whipped with a small amount of sugar for a fluffier texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cream in the refrigerator at 1 °C‑4 °C in its original container. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Light vanilla ice cream is a low‑calorie dessert made from skimmed milk, natural vanilla extract, and a small amount of sweeteners. It retains a creamy taste while containing far less fat and sugar than traditional ice cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light ice cream is often used in diet plans and weight‑loss programs.
The vanilla flavor comes from real vanilla bean seeds, not artificial aromatics.
To keep a smooth texture with reduced fat, stabilizers are added to the formulation.
Common sweeteners include stevia, erythritol, and sucralose, all of which have a low glycemic index.
A lactose‑free version can be made with lactose‑free milk, making it suitable for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Low Calorie Content
items.content: Because of reduced fat and sugar, a serving provides roughly 100–120 kcal, helping to maintain an energy balance.

items.title: Source of Calcium
items.content: Skimmed milk used in the recipe retains a high calcium level, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dairy provides vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting metabolic processes.

items.title: Low Glycemic Index
items.content: Low‑GI sweeteners do not cause sharp spikes in blood glucose.

items.title: Probiotic Content (in some versions)
items.content: If yogurt or kefir is used, the ice cream can help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Milk Protein Allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Artificial Sweeteners
items.content: Large amounts of sugar alcohols (erythritol, xylitol) may cause digestive discomfort in some individuals.

items.title: Stabilizer Content
items.content: Additives such as carrageenan or guar gum can trigger gastrointestinal reactions in sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve light vanilla ice cream in individual cups, as a standalone dessert, or paired with berries, nuts, and whole‑grain cereals. It works well in smoothies, as a base for fruit parfaits, or as a cold sauce for baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the ice cream in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, seal the container tightly to prevent ice crystal formation. Do not store more than 2–3 months beyond the printed date.

rice-white-with-dark-green-vegetables-no.title: White Rice with Dark Green Vegetables, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice mixed with dark green vegetables (such as broccoli, spinach or green beans) without any added fat. It is rich in carbohydrates, fiber, B‑vitamins and provides plant antioxidants from the vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.
Dark green vegetables contain chlorophyll, which gives them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
The lack of added fat makes the dish low‑calorie, suitable for weight management.
Combining rice with vegetables offers a longer feeling of fullness by mixing fast and slow‑digesting carbs.
The recipe can be adapted to various cuisines by adding spices, soy sauce or herbs.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy thanks to easily digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Dark green vegetables supply vitamin K, vitamin C, folate and potassium.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables promotes intestinal motility and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Phytonutrients in green vegetables help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Although rare, rice allergy can occur and requires avoidance of the product.

items.title: Lack of fat
items.content: Without fat, the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables may be reduced; consider adding a small amount of healthy fat elsewhere in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish as a side or a standalone meal. It reheats well in the microwave; add soy sauce, lemon juice or fresh herbs for flavor. Pair with lean protein such as chicken, tofu or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it keeps for up to 2 months after cooling and placing in a freezer‑safe bag.

squash-summer-casserole-with-rice-and-to.title: Summer Squash Casserole with Rice and Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash is a tender variety harvested in warm months. The casserole combines cubed squash, cooked rice, and tomato sauce, baked until golden. The dish balances the mild sweetness of squash with the savory tang of tomatoes and the heartiness of rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash contains less sugar than autumn varieties, giving it a delicate flavor.
Tomato sauce adds lycopene, a powerful antioxidant, to the casserole.
Squash is rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Casseroles with squash and rice are traditional in Mediterranean cuisine as a light summer meal.
Baking retains most of the squash’s vitamins and minerals.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in squash supports vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Tomato sauce provides lycopene and potassium, which help maintain healthy blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies steady energy release and helps stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dish is prepared with minimal added oil, making it suitable for light eating.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Squash and rice contribute fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Squash allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to squash.

items.title: Sodium in sauce
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains salt; choose a low‑sodium version if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Rice glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index; consider using brown rice or quinoa for a lower impact.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the casserole hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or basil. Sprinkle grated cheese on top a few minutes before the end of baking for extra flavor. Pair with a simple green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the casserole to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to retain the crispy topping.
